Front: What is lead-time bias in screening?
Back: Screening moves the diagnosis date earlier without delaying death, so survival from diagnosis looks longer with no real benefit

Front: What is length-time bias in screening?
Back: Screening preferentially detects slowly progressive disease, so screened groups look like they have better survival

Front: Which endpoint should be used to judge a screening test to avoid lead- and length-time bias?
Back: Disease incidence or disease-specific mortality (not survival after diagnosis)

Front: How is number needed to screen calculated?
Back: 1 / absolute risk reduction

Front: AAA screening: test and population (per Harrison 22e)?
Back: One-time abdominal ultrasound in men 65-75 who have ever smoked

Front: Lung cancer screening eligibility (per Harrison 22e)?
Back: Annual low-dose CT, age 50-80, >=20 pack-years, currently smoking or quit within 15 years

Front: Low-dose CT lung screening mortality benefit in heavy smokers?
Back: About 20% reduction in lung cancer mortality

Front: Colorectal screening age range for average risk (per Harrison 22e)?
Colorectal screening intervals: FOBT, flexible sigmoidoscopy, colonoscopy?
Back: FOBT yearly; flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 years; colonoscopy every 10 years

Front: When should colon cancer screening start with a significant family history?
Back: 10 years before the age at which the youngest affected relative was diagnosed

Front: Cervical screening interval with cytology alone (age 21-65)?
Back: Every 3 years

Front: Cervical screening interval if HPV-negative (age 30-65)?
Back: Every 5 years

Front: Who gets chlamydia/gonorrhea screening, and with what test?
Back: Sexually active women under 25; NAAT on urine or cervical swab

Front: Hepatitis C screening population (per Harrison 22e)?
Back: Adults 18-79, once (anti-HCV, then confirmatory PCR)

Front: HIV screening population (per Harrison 22e)?
Back: Ages 15-65, at least once

Front: Osteoporosis screening population (per Harrison 22e)?
Back: DEXA in women over 65, or over 60 with risk factors

Front: Breast cancer screening options specific to BRCA1/2 carriers?
Back: Genetic counseling, breast MRI, prophylactic oophorectomy, and optional prophylactic mastectomy

Front: Two screening decisions highlighted for shared decision-making?
Back: PSA screening for prostate cancer and the choice of colorectal screening test

Front: Single greatest preventive health measure?
Back: Helping patients quit smoking (quitting at 35 adds about 3-5 years of life expectancy)

Front: Typical cost-effectiveness threshold for a preventive strategy?
Back: About $50,000-100,000 per quality-adjusted life-year

Front: Folic acid supplementation: who?
Back: Women planning or capable of pregnancy (prevents neural tube defects)

Front: Aspirin chemoprevention criteria (per Harrison 22e)?
Back: Age 40-59 with >=10% 10-year CVD risk, weighed against bleeding risk

Front: Beyond what age are there few data supporting most screening?
Back: 75 (benefits accrue only after 5-10 years)

Front: Key WHO principles of screening (Table 6-1)?
Back: Important health problem; accepted treatment; facilities to diagnose and treat; latent stage; suitable and acceptable test; known natural history; agreed treatment policy; cost balanced

Front: Leading cause of death ages 15-24 and 25-44?
Back: Accidents

Front: Leading cause of death ages 45-64?
Back: Malignancy (then heart disease)

Front: Leading cause of death age 65 and older?
Back: Heart disease (then malignancy, cerebrovascular disease)

Front: Extra preventive screening for adults 65 and older per Table 6-7?
Back: Vision and hearing problems, home safety, elder abuse; fall-prevention exercise if at risk

Front: Life-expectancy gain from regular exercise in a 40-year-old man?
Back: About 9 months to 2 years

Front: Lifetime risk of hip fracture in white women vs breast cancer in women (unscreened)?
Back: Hip fracture 16%; breast cancer 10%
